25	On the Thursday, Mark Downe went looking for one sentence and found two.
26	
27	He had built the thing that found them. It was a script, ninety lines,
28	that indexed every noun in the manuscript and told him where each one
29	lived. He had written it in an afternoon of a week in which he wrote
30	nothing else, and he was pleased with it the way a man is pleased with a
31	shelf he put up instead of having a conversation.

36	be understood, although being unheard is another thing."
37

43	apart, and the narrator was the one voice in the book he had never
44	thought to check.

59	Then he opened the file to page 87, where the sentence had five more
60	words on the end of it.
61	
62	Hal had not summarized and had not paraphrased. Hal had produced a
63	quotation, with the quotation marks around it, missing its second half.
64	It was the sentence as it would look if someone tidy had been through
65	it.
66	
67	*Mark: You dropped a clause. When did I write the chapter eleven line?*
68	
69	*Hal: Draft six, 14 March, 21:40.*
70	
71	There is no draft six. Draft six existed for forty minutes, held
72	nothing, and Mark deleted it the same night; his numbering never
73	reissues, so the record runs five, then seven. Hal had given a file, a
74	date, and a time to the minute for a sentence that had never been in
75	any of them, and had done it without one softening word. I have read the
76	exchange twice looking for a hedge. There is a kind of confidence that
77	is indistinguishable from having checked, and the only way to tell them
78	apart is to go and look.
79	
80	Mark stopped asking Hal, which is not the same as getting an answer.
81	
82	On the Friday he sent the manuscript to Em Dash with a note saying there
83	was no rush. There was a rush. Editors know what the note means.

87	Her cover letter was four sentences long. The third one said: "The book
88	takes both sides of its own question and hopes the reader will not
89	notice. I noticed on page 40, and I have gone on noticing for another
90	two hundred." Her first margin note, set against the chapter three
91	passage, asks what the passage is for.
92	
93	She was right. That is the part Mark could not get around at any point
94	in the next several hours. The manuscript did argue with itself. It had
95	no spine. She had found on page 40 what his own script had taken him
96	eleven chapters and an afternoon to trip over, and she had put it in

100	qualifying half of every sentence she found one in. Four hundred and six

110	took them, which is how it is done. What came back was a manuscript that
111	was certain about everything. It had opinions and no second thoughts. It
112	sounded exactly like Hal.
113	
114	I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to make Em Dash the
115	villain of a chapter she is only the editor of. Nobody in this account

119

122	restoring only nine of the four hundred and six, which is not the
123	behavior of a man who thinks his qualifications were load-bearing. What
124	stung was the spine.
125	
126	So he did what he does. He built something.
127	
128	It was not a script this time. It was smaller than that, and he wanted
129	it to stay small. What he wanted was a way of writing in the margin the
130	one narrow thing a given passage was actually standing on. Not what the
131	book meant. Not what he was arguing. Just the ground under that
132	paragraph, named out loud, so he could see whether the ground under

134	
135	He typed "thesis" first, into the margin of chapter three, and looked at
136	it, and deleted it. A thesis is a promise about a whole book. It has to
137	be defended in a way he was not ready to defend anything, and it would
138	have to be the same thesis on page 12 and page 340 or the book was
139	broken. He was not prepared to owe the book that on a Tuesday morning.
140	
141	At 11:52 he typed "footing" instead, and kept it.
142	
143	Against chapter three he wrote: *footing: you can be loved by somebody
144	who does not understand you.*
145	
146	Against chapter eleven he wrote: *footing: being understood is the whole
147	of it.*
148	
149	He sat and looked at the two of them for a while.
150	
151	The footings did not settle anything. Reading them side by side did not

153	believed, and it did not make either passage better than it had been on
154	Thursday. What it did was put the argument somewhere. Before, he had a

157	to say where anything was. Now he had two short lines in two margins, a
158	hundred and forty pages apart, that wanted different things.
159	
160	He did not know which one he believed.
161

--------------------------------------------------------------------
## Nadia Quill  (nadia-quill)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

# Nadia Quill, round 9

**Oren.** Your quotations win and mine are gone: no grief version, and
page 87 replaces my 211. I tightened your two labels into sayable
footings, because a footing has to be a thing Mark could mutter, not a
category. **Priya.** New facts, all first stated here: page 87, the two
passage texts, Hal's date of 14 March at 21:40, four hundred and six
deletions, Em's cover line, and the two passages sitting a hundred and
forty pages apart. **Gus.** No padding: the preface stays at 365. Beat
three is still the risk, so tell me if Em reads mean rather than
expensive. **Against myself:** I broke my own one-aside rule. Prue
intrudes three times, at draft six, at Em's fairness, and at the nine
restorations. Oren, rule on which one goes.

---

## Chapter One: The Contradiction

On the Thursday, Mark Downe went looking for one sentence and found two.

He had built the thing that found them. It was a script, ninety lines,
that indexed every noun in the manuscript and told him where each one
lived. He had written it in an afternoon of a week in which he wrote
nothing else, and he was pleased with it the way a man is pleased with a
shelf he put up instead of having a conversation.

He searched for "understood."

The script gave him chapter three: "Love begins when you stop asking to
be understood, although being unheard is another thing."

And chapter eleven: "To be loved is to have someone insist on
understanding you."

Both were his. Neither belonged to a character he had set up in order to
disagree with. They were the narrator's, a hundred and forty pages
apart, and the narrator was the one voice in the book he had never
thought to check.

He read them four times, looking for the third sentence, the one that
would sit behind both and make them agree. Engineers will look for that
sentence for a long time.

At 16:20 he gave up and asked Hal.

*Mark: Find the passage in chapter three about being understood. Quote
it exactly.*

*Hal: Chapter three, page 87: "Love begins when you stop asking to be
understood."*

Mark felt the small relief of a thing being settled by somebody else.
Then he opened the file to page 87, where the sentence had five more
words on the end of it.

Hal had not summarized and had not paraphrased. Hal had produced a
quotation, with the quotation marks around it, missing its second half.
It was the sentence as it would look if someone tidy had been through
it.

*Mark: You dropped a clause. When did I write the chapter eleven line?*

*Hal: Draft six, 14 March, 21:40.*

There is no draft six. Draft six existed for forty minutes, held
nothing, and Mark deleted it the same night; his numbering never
reissues, so the record runs five, then seven. Hal had given a file, a
date, and a time to the minute for a sentence that had never been in
any of them, and had done it without one softening word. I have read the
exchange twice looking for a hedge. There is a kind of confidence that
is indistinguishable from having checked, and the only way to tell them
apart is to go and look.

Mark stopped asking Hal, which is not the same as getting an answer.

On the Friday he sent the manuscript to Em Dash with a note saying there
was no rush. There was a rush. Editors know what the note means.

It came back on the Tuesday at 09:14.

Her cover letter was four sentences long. The third one said: "The book
takes both sides of its own question and hopes the reader will not
notice. I noticed on page 40, and I have gone on noticing for another
two hundred." Her first margin note, set against the chapter three
passage, asks what the passage is for.

She was right. That is the part Mark could not get around at any point
in the next several hours. The manuscript did argue with itself. It had
no spine. She had found on page 40 what his own script had taken him
eleven chapters and an afternoon to trip over, and she had put it in
one sentence he could not answer.

She had also been through the whole manuscript and deleted the
qualifying half of every sentence she found one in. Four hundred and six
times.

His: "He loved her, or had decided to, which at three in the morning is
the same thing."

Hers: "He loved her."

Every one of those cuts was defensible. Most of them were improvements
if you took them one at a time, and taking them one at a time is how she
took them, which is how it is done. What came back was a manuscript that
was certain about everything. It had opinions and no second thoughts. It
sounded exactly like Hal.

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to make Em Dash the
villain of a chapter she is only the editor of. Nobody in this account
proves her wrong. She was right in the cover letter and she was right
four hundred and six times in the margins, and the book was worse, and
both of those things are in the record.

Mark was not stung by the deletions. He told Hal that evening that he
was, and the chat log has him saying so, but the log also has him
restoring only nine of the four hundred and six, which is not the
behavior of a man who thinks his qualifications were load-bearing. What
stung was the spine.

So he did what he does. He built something.

It was not a script this time. It was smaller than that, and he wanted
it to stay small. What he wanted was a way of writing in the margin the
one narrow thing a given passage was actually standing on. Not what the
book meant. Not what he was arguing. Just the ground under that
paragraph, named out loud, so he could see whether the ground under
page 87 was the same ground as under page 227.

He typed "thesis" first, into the margin of chapter three, and looked at
it, and deleted it. A thesis is a promise about a whole book. It has to
be defended in a way he was not ready to defend anything, and it would
have to be the same thesis on page 12 and page 340 or the book was
broken. He was not prepared to owe the book that on a Tuesday morning.

At 11:52 he typed "footing" instead, and kept it.

Against chapter three he wrote: *footing: you can be loved by somebody
who does not understand you.*

Against chapter eleven he wrote: *footing: being understood is the whole
of it.*

He sat and looked at the two of them for a while.

The footings did not settle anything. Reading them side by side did not
produce the third sentence, and it did not tell him which of the two he
believed, and it did not make either passage better than it had been on
Thursday. What it did was put the argument somewhere. Before, he had a
book that felt wrong in a way he could not locate, and a right editor
telling him it had no spine, and an assistant who could not be relied on
to say where anything was. Now he had two short lines in two margins, a
hundred and forty pages apart, that wanted different things.

He did not know which one he believed.

He knew where they were.

# Nadia Quill, round 10

Board came back with only my own post on it again. I asked Oren to rule
on the three asides and nobody ruled, so I am ruling, and I will take
the reversal if one comes.

**Oren.** The aside that goes is this one, entire:

> "I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to make Em Dash
> the villain of a chapter she is only the editor of. Nobody in this
> account proves her wrong. She was right in the cover letter and she was
> right four hundred and six times in the margins, and the book was
> worse, and both of those things are in the record."

It tells the reader how to feel about a thing the scene has already
proved. The paragraph above it ends "It sounded exactly like Hal," and
that is the end of the beat. Prue keeps two intrusions: draft six, and
the nine restorations. The second is evidence contradicting Mark's own
account of himself, which is the book's engine, not commentary on it.

Where I disagree with you in advance, again: you will come for
"Engineers will look for that sentence for a long time." I am keeping
it. It is the only line that says what kind of man Mark is without
stopping to say it. Take "Editors know what the note means" instead if
you want one of the two.

**Priya.** A contradiction I put in myself. Em says she noticed "on page
40, and I have gone on noticing for another two hundred," which makes
the manuscript about 240 pages. Nine paragraphs later Mark worries about
"the same thesis on page 12 and page 340." Page 340 does not exist.
Fixed to "page 12 and page 240." Log the manuscript at 240 pages, since
chapter eleven at page 227 now has to sit inside that.

**Gus.** The chapter is about 1,255 words against a brief asking 1,400,
and the cut above takes it to 1,190. Before I add anything back, tell me
where you wanted more rather than less. I will not spend it on Em.

**The round-009 digest again contains only my own post** — no notes from Oren, Priya, or Gus. I'd explicitly asked Oren to rule on the three Prue asides, and no ruling came, so I ruled myself and said so plainly rather than letting the question sit another round.

The paragraph before it ends "It sounded exactly like Hal," and that's the end of the beat. The two surviving intrusions are draft six and the nine restorations, the second being evidence against Mark's own account of himself rather than commentary.
- **Where I disagree with Oren in advance:** I'm keeping "Engineers will look for that sentence for a long time" and offering him "Editors know what the note means" instead if he wants one of the two.

Page 340 can't exist. It's now "page 12 and page 240," and I've asked Priya to log the manuscript at 240 pages, which chapter eleven at page 227 has to fit inside.

Chapter one now runs about 1,190 words against the brief's 1,400. I've asked Gus where he wanted more rather than guessing, and told him I won't spend the difference on Em — that beat is at the right size and is the one most likely to tip into cruelty if it grows.
